# Contracts and components

> How a contract you write as data becomes a typed, accessible React component you can read.
>
> **This is the Markdown mirror.** The [interactive version](../05-contracts.html) has live
> widgets — a brand switch, an alias-chain walker, a pipeline stepper, and a quiz — that
> Markdown cannot render.

← [Tokens and brands](04-tokens.md)  ·  [Contents](README.md)  ·  [The code](06-the-code.md) →

---

A contract describes a component: its variants, its states, which tokens it uses, how it behaves
for assistive technology, and how far a consumer may extend it. You write it in TypeScript for the
autocomplete. girih treats it as data.

This is the longest chapter here, and most people arrive at it holding one specific question rather
than wanting to read ten sections. If that is you:

| You want to | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Add a variant, size or state to a component | [Anatomy](#anatomy) — every field, and what each one does to the output |
| Work out why a token reference fails to validate | [Cross-validation](#validation) — especially if it only fails for one brand |
| Vary a component without forking it | [Extensions](#extensions) — `defineVariant` and its limits |
| Hand-write the markup for one component | [Ejection](#eject) — forking as a recorded operation |
| Understand a version bump you did not expect | [Versioning](#semver) — what feeds the signature |
| Know why `.ds/ir/` is committed to your repo | [The IR](#ir) — and why it is deleted on every generate |

Read start to finish and it goes: what a contract is, what girih turns it into, then what you can do
to one after it exists.

## What a contract is

`defineSpec()` looks like a function call and is really a declaration. It does not run
logic, branch on anything, or produce a component at runtime — it returns a plain object that
girih validates, converts to a canonical form, diffs against the last published version, and
compiles.

> **🔵 Rule — Contracts are data, not code**
>
> TypeScript is the authoring surface because it gives you autocomplete on token paths — the
> generated `tokens.d.ts` exports a `TokenPath` union of every real token, so
> a typo is a type error before it is a build error. But the contract must remain pure data: no
> function values, no imports of runtime code, no environment branching. Everything girih can do
> with contracts — validate, diff, version, compile to multiple targets — depends on being able to
> read them without executing them.

> **🟢 In plain words**
>
> A contract is a specification, like a blueprint. It says "a Button has three variants, three
> sizes, uses these tokens, and is focusable". It does not _make_ a button any more than a
> blueprint makes a house. girih is the builder, and the blueprint is what lets it check its work.

## Anatomy of a contract

Here is the real Button contract from the example workspace, in full:

**design/components/button/button.contract.ts  [You write this]**

```ts
import { defineSpec } from '@faravahar/girih';

export default defineSpec({
  name: 'Button',
  description: 'Triggers an action. Single-line label.',
  element: 'button',

  variants: {
    variant: { values: ['primary', 'secondary', 'danger'], default: 'primary' },
    size: { values: ['sm', 'md', 'lg'], default: 'md' },
  },
  states: ['hover', 'focus-visible', 'disabled', 'loading'],

  slots: { children: { required: true } },

  tokens: {
    base: {
      fontFamily: '{typography.body-family}',
      borderRadius: '{button.radius}',
    },
    variants: {
      variant: {
        primary: {
          background: '{button.primary.background}',
          color: '{button.primary.foreground}',
          states: {
            hover: { background: '{button.primary.background-hover}' },
          },
        },
        secondary: {
          background: '{button.secondary.background}',
          color: '{button.secondary.foreground}',
          borderColor: '{button.secondary.border}',
        },
        danger: {
          background: '{button.danger.background}',
          color: '{button.danger.foreground}',
          states: {
            hover: { background: '{button.danger.background-hover}' },
          },
        },
      },
      size: {
        sm: { height: '{button.size.sm.height}', paddingInline: '{control.padding-inline-sm}', fontSize: '{typography.size-sm}' },
        md: { height: '{button.size.md.height}', paddingInline: '{control.padding-inline-md}', fontSize: '{typography.size-md}' },
        lg: { height: '{button.size.lg.height}', paddingInline: '{control.padding-inline-lg}', fontSize: '{typography.size-lg}' },
      },
    },
  },

  accessibility: {
    focusable: true,
    aria: {
      loading: { 'aria-busy': 'true' },
    },
  },

  extensibility: {
    allowExtends: true,
    overridableTokens: ['background', 'color', 'borderColor'],
  },
});

```

Field by field:

| Field | What it declares | Consequence in the output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | PascalCase component name | The exported identifier and the CSS class (`.ds-button`) |
| `element` | The underlying DOM element | Which template is chosen, and what props are inherited |
| `variants` | Named axes with values and a default | A TypeScript union per axis plus a `data-*` attribute |
| `states` | Interaction states to express | CSS selectors — `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `[data-loading]` |
| `slots` | Content holes and whether they are required | `children` typing |
| `tokens` | Which token drives which CSS property | Every declaration in `components.css` |
| `accessibility` | Focusability and state→ARIA mapping | `aria-busy`, `aria-disabled`, focus ring |
| `extensibility` | Whether it may be extended, and which tokens | What `defineVariant` is allowed to override |

> **🟡 Watch out — Nested states inside variants**
>
> Look at the `primary` variant: it has its own `states` block with a
> `hover` entry. That is how "the primary button gets darker on hover, but the secondary
> one does not" is expressed. It compiles to
> `.ds-button[data-variant="primary"]:hover` — a variant-scoped state selector — rather
> than a blanket hover rule. The secondary variant has no hover entry, so no such rule is emitted
> for it.

## Contract to component

| # | Stage | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Load** | jiti imports the .contract.ts |
| 2 | **To IR** | specToIR() canonicalises |
| 3 | **Validate** | against every brand graph |
| 4 | **Template** | pick by element + capability |
| 5 | **Emit TSX** | typed, a11y-wired component |
| 6 | **Emit CSS** | structure only, all var() |

`jiti` is what lets girih import a TypeScript file at runtime without a build step —
which is necessary because your contract is `.ts` and girih is running as a compiled
binary that has never seen your source.

## The IR: why an intermediate form

Between the contract and the generator sits `ComponentIR` — a canonical, target-neutral
form written to `.ds/ir/.json`. It is generated, and it is
_committed_, which surprises people.

**.ds/ir/button.json (excerpt of the real file)  [girih writes this]**

```json
{
  "name": "Button",
  "template": "element",
  "element": "button",
  "variants": [
    { "axis": "variant", "values": ["primary", "secondary", "danger"], "default": "primary" },
    { "axis": "size", "values": ["sm", "md", "lg"], "default": "md" }
  ],
  "states": ["hover", "focus-visible", "disabled", "loading"],
  "childrenRequired": true,
  "tokens": {
    "base": [
      { "property": "font-family",    "ref": "{typography.body-family}" },
      { "property": "border-radius",  "ref": "{button.radius}" }
    ],
    "variants": [
      { "axis": "variant", "value": "primary",
        "declarations": [
          { "property": "background", "ref": "{button.primary.background}" },
          { "property": "color",      "ref": "{button.primary.foreground}" }
        ],
        "states": [
          { "state": "hover",
            "declarations": [{ "property": "background", "ref": "{button.primary.background-hover}" }] }
        ] }
    ]
  },
  "accessibility": { "focusable": true, "aria": [{ "state": "loading", "attributes": { "aria-busy": "true" } }] },
  "extensibility": { "allowExtends": true, "overridableTokens": ["background", "color", "borderColor"] },
  "sourceFile": "design/components/button/button.contract.ts"
}
```

The IR exists for three reasons, and they are all about decoupling:

1. **Multiple targets, one shape.** A future Figma generator should consume one  canonical form rather than re-reading and re-interpreting `.contract.ts` files. The React  generator already only sees IR — it has no idea TypeScript was involved.
2. **Reviewable diffs.** Reorganising your spec file without changing its meaning  produces no IR diff. Changing the component's public surface always does. In a pull request the  IR diff is the honest answer to "what changed for consumers?"
3. **Diffable for versioning.** The semver machinery compares signatures computed from  IR. Canonical form means a formatting change cannot masquerade as a version bump.

> **🟡 Watch out — The IR directory is fully derived — so girih deletes it before writing**
>
> On each `generate react`, girih removes `.ds/ir/` entirely and rewrites it.
> If it merged instead, renaming a component would leave the old JSON behind forever, and the
> signature diff would think a component still exists that does not. Wholesale replacement is the
> only correct move for a directory that is purely a function of its inputs.

## What comes out

Two files per component. First the React component — this is the real emitted output, not a
simplification:

**packages/design-system/src/button.tsx  [girih writes this]**

```tsx
/* Generated by girih — do not edit. Source of truth: components/button.contract.ts */
import { forwardRef } from 'react';
import type { ComponentPropsWithoutRef } from 'react';
import { cx } from '@faravahar/girih-react-runtime';

export type ButtonVariant = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger';
export type ButtonSize = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';

export interface ButtonProps extends Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>, 'variant' | 'size'> {
  variant?: ButtonVariant;
  size?: ButtonSize;
  loading?: boolean;
}

/** Triggers an action. Single-line label. */
export const Button = forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(function Button(
  { variant = 'primary', size = 'md', loading = false, className, disabled, type = 'button', children, ...rest },
  ref,
) {
  return (
    <button
      ref={ref}
      className={cx('ds-button', className)}
      data-variant={variant}
      data-size={size}
      data-loading={loading || undefined}
      aria-busy={loading ? 'true' : undefined}
      disabled={disabled || loading}
      type={type}
      {...rest}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
});

```

Read what the contract bought you:

- `ButtonVariant` and `ButtonSize` are string-literal unions — passing  `"tertiary"` is a type error at the call site.
- `Omit, 'variant' | 'size'>` means every  native button prop works, with the two the contract claims removed so they cannot conflict.
- `data-variant` and `data-size` are the styling hooks — no class-name  concatenation, no CSS-in-JS.
- `aria-busy` when loading, and `disabled || loading` so a loading button  cannot be clicked. That came from the `accessibility` block, not from the generator  guessing.
- `forwardRef` throughout, so the component composes with focus management and  positioning libraries.

And the CSS — structure and token references, nothing else:

**styles/components.css — real output  [girih writes this]**

```css
.ds-button {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  border: 1px solid transparent;
  font: inherit;
  cursor: pointer;
  text-decoration: none;
}

.ds-button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

.ds-button:disabled,
.ds-button[aria-disabled="true"],
.ds-button[data-loading="true"] {
  cursor: not-allowed;
  opacity: 0.55;
}

.ds-button {
  font-family: var(--ds-typography-body-family);
  border-radius: var(--ds-button-radius);
}

.ds-button[data-variant="primary"] {
  background: var(--ds-button-primary-background);
  color: var(--ds-button-primary-foreground);
}
```

> **🔵 Rule — Every design value is a var(). No exceptions.**
>
> Notice what is hardcoded: `display`, `align-items`,
> `cursor`, `outline-offset`, `opacity: 0.55`. All structural or
> behavioural. Every value a designer would want to change — colour, radius, font, spacing, size —
> is a `var()`.
>
> This is the property that makes one `components.css` serve every brand. The structure
> is brand-independent by construction, so there is nothing to duplicate per brand.

## Cross-validation against every brand

`validateSpecs(irs, build.graphs, TEMPLATE_REGISTRY)` takes the resolved token graphs
for _all_ brands. That plural is the whole point.

> **🔴 Important — The most common real defect in this area**
>
> A token reference that resolves under the default brand but not under another one. It is easy to
> create: you add `{color.tertiary}`, it works locally because you are on the default
> brand, and the second brand has no such token. Because validation runs against every graph, this
> is a build error rather than a production surprise — and the diagnostic is prefixed with the
> brand name, so you know which one is missing it.

| Validation | Range | What it rejects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name shape | `GIRIH4001` | A component name that is not PascalCase — it becomes an exported identifier |
| Unknown token ref | `GIRIH4030`+ | A `{token}` that no brand can resolve |
| Reserved prop | `GIRIH4010`+ | A variant axis colliding with a React or generator prop |
| Unimplementable state | `GIRIH4020`+ | A state the chosen template cannot express |
| Variant default | `GIRIH4005`+ | A default that is not one of the declared values |
| Extension overreach | `GIRIH4040`+ | An extension overriding a token outside `overridableTokens` |

There are 32 codes in the `GIRIH4xxx` range — more than
any other family — because a contract has the largest surface area of anything a user writes. The
full list with messages is in [chapter 07](07-error-codes.md).

---

Everything above is what a contract _is_ and what girih makes of it. The rest of this chapter
is what you do to one that already exists: extend it, fork it, and ship the result.

## Extensions

Sometimes a consumer needs a variation the design system did not anticipate. The wrong answer is a
fork. The girih answer is `defineVariant`: a declaration that extends an existing
component within limits the base contract set.

**design/components/button/payment-button.ext.ts  [You write this]**

```ts
import { defineVariant } from '@faravahar/girih';

export default defineVariant({
  name: 'PaymentButton',
  extends: 'Button',
  description: 'Checkout call-to-action — high-contrast, brand-independent emphasis.',
  tokens: {
    background: '{color.text}',
    color: '{color.background}',
  },
});

```

That compiles to a component that is a thin wrapper over the base, plus a scoped CSS rule:

**packages/design-system/src/payment-button.tsx  [girih writes this]**

```tsx
/* Generated by girih — do not edit. Source of truth: design/components/button/payment-button.ext.ts */
import { forwardRef } from 'react';
import { cx } from '@faravahar/girih-react-runtime';
import { Button } from './button';
import type { ButtonProps } from './button';

/** Checkout call-to-action — high-contrast, brand-independent emphasis. */
export const PaymentButton = forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(function PaymentButton(
  { className, ...rest },
  ref,
) {
  return <Button ref={ref} className={cx('ds-x-payment-button', className)} {...rest} />;
});

```

It inherits `ButtonProps` exactly, so every variant and size still works, and it adds
one class that overrides two tokens. Which two it is allowed to override is not the extension's
choice — the Button's contract declares
`overridableTokens: ['background', 'color', 'borderColor']`, and an extension reaching
outside that list is a build error.

> **🟡 Watch out — You cannot eject an extension**
>
> `girih eject PaymentButton` refuses, and the error explains why: extensions are pure
> data and always regenerated, so there is nothing to fork. Edit the `.ext.ts`. If you
> need to fork the _markup_, you eject the base component instead.

## Templates and the Dialog problem

Most components are one element with attributes — a template called `element` handles
Button, Badge, Card, Input. But a Dialog needs focus trapping, scroll locking, escape handling and
correct ARIA relationships across several nodes. That is not markup; it is behaviour, and writing
it from scratch is how accessibility bugs are born.

girih's Dialog is built on [Base UI](https://base-ui.com), behind a swappable adapter in
`src/internal/headless.ts`. The contract does not mention Base UI at all.

> **🔵 Rule — Why the adapter matters**
>
> Headless primitive libraries are young and they churn — the version pinned here is
> `1.0.0-rc.0`. If the contract named Base UI directly, swapping it would be a breaking
> change for every consumer. Behind an adapter, the underlying library is an implementation detail
> of the generated package: the contract, the emitted API, and the token surface all stay put.

The `TEMPLATE_REGISTRY` records what each template can express, along with a version
number. Contract validation consults it — which is how "this state is unimplementable" becomes a
build error instead of a silently missing CSS rule. The version number matters for ejection, next.

## Ejection: the tracked fork

Occasionally a component genuinely needs hand-written markup. Every generator that pretends
otherwise gets forked in the dark. girih's answer is to make forking a first-class, recorded
operation.

**[Terminal]**

```
$ pnpm exec girih eject Dialog

create  design/components/dialog/dialog.ejected.tsx
update  ds.lock (base: dialog@v1, 4f2a9c1e8b03)

'Dialog' is now yours: edit design/components/dialog/dialog.ejected.tsx freely — commit it and ds.lock.
Its spec is still validated and its CSS still generated — only markup/behavior is forked.
Run `girih generate react` to stitch it into the package.
```

Four things happen, and each one is doing specific work:

1. The current template output is written to  `design/components/dialog/dialog.ejected.tsx` — beside the contract it forks, your  file now, committed to git.
2. `ds.lock` records the template name, the template _version_, and a hash of the  exact source the fork started from.
3. Subsequent `generate` runs stitch your file into the package instead of the  template's output.
4. The spec is still validated and the CSS is still generated from it. You forked the markup, not  the token governance.

> **🟡 Watch out — Ejecting is also the drift gate’s own remedy**
>
> If the generated file on disk already had hand edits when you ejected, girih carries
> _those_ into the fork rather than the pristine template output — and says so. Following
> the drift gate's advice must never lose your work. The recorded `baseHash` stays
> pristine regardless, because that hash is what a future three-way merge would rebase against.

`girih forks` reports forks that have drifted from their recorded base, on two axes:
the template version moved, or the spec changed since the eject. The three-way merge itself is not
implemented — the command tells you honestly that it is a report, not a fix.

## Versioning from the contract diff

Because a contract is data in canonical form, two versions of it can be compared mechanically. So
girih does not ask you what version to publish. It computes one.

| Change | Bump | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A token value changed | `patch` | Consumers see different pixels, same API |
| A new variant, size, state or component | `minor` | Additive — existing code keeps working |
| Anything removed or renamed | `major` | Some consumer call site is now invalid |
| Nothing changed | `none` | Publishing would be noise; the command says so and stops |

The signature hashed for comparison is broader than the specs alone. From
`computeSignature()`: the resolved token graphs per brand, the component IRs, the
extensions, the template versions, the ejected sources, and the emitted file set. Three
consequences worth internalising:

- A template version bump moves the signature even with no contract edit — because the emitted markup changed.
- Editing an ejected fork affects the published package, so it affects the bump.
- A token value change in _any_ brand counts, not only the default one.

**[Terminal]**

```
$ pnpm exec girih bake --check

@acme/design-system  0.2.1 → 0.3.0  [minor]
  Button: variant 'tertiary' added
  Badge: token 'badge.primary.background' value changed
  …

Run `girih bake` to stage 0.3.0 into .ds/baked and commit it as the new baseline.

$ pnpm exec girih bake

baked @acme/design-system@0.3.0 → .ds/baked
Publish it however you like, e.g. `npm publish .ds/baked`.
```

> **🔴 Important — girih bake commits a version the moment it finds one — --check is the safe preview**
>
> `girih bake --check` only computes and prints the bump; it stages nothing and
> writes nothing. Bare `girih bake` builds the package, stages a bumped
> `package.json` + `dist/` + `styles/` into
> `.ds/baked`, and commits that version into `ds.lock` as the new
> baseline — all in one step, with no further confirmation, since there is no npm call left
> to gate on.
>
> Publishing `.ds/baked` itself is entirely yours: `npm publish .ds/baked`,
> `pnpm publish`, or pointing your own registry config at that folder all work — girih
> never touches a registry. The one thing worth knowing if you publish scoped packages: a scoped
> package's _first_ publish is restricted by default on npm and needs
> `--access public`, whichever tool you publish with.

That is the model, end to end. [Chapter 06](06-the-code.md) maps it onto the actual
packages, so you know where to look when something misbehaves.
